title: TiDB, One Layer at a Time: How Distributed SQL Became an Agentic AI Backbone

segments.text: Yeah, hello and welcome. I'm Matthias Johnson. I work as a principal software engineer at PingCAP working on the TiDB, which is a distributed SQL database
fully transactional. Uh before TiDB, I worked also at booking.com. So I've seen MySQL installation at really high scale. And before that, I worked at
developer at MySQL mostly coding in the table partition engine. And this is Daniel. He'll take the first part of the presentation. >> Yes. So I'm Daniel van Eeden.
Um also working for TiDB. I'm working as a technical support engineer. So I help our customers to get the most out of our product. But besides this, I do many
other things wearing multiple hats. Um I've also been working at booking.com just at uh Sherlock. Um so I also know how it is to run databases at like a really high
scale, high volume scenario. So the very first thing we're going to start off with today is to discuss the problem that we're actually solving with
this product. So the the base problem is the single box ceiling. So you start with your single machine database, maybe a few copies as like
a backup. But then you grow more. And like one of the things that the people start to do is to use read replicas. So on the on the left on this page, you
see the read replicas. So basically, your application needs to like split the reads and the writes. So the writes go to the the primary, the
reads go to the replicas. So that's a bit of work for the application to split out. But once you've done this, you can more easily
scale out your whole database. Um the main thing here is that the primary and the replicas have asynchronous replication. Um, this can be with MySQL, this can be
with Postgres, with any other database. Um, but it means that the the reach you do from the replicas might have um, a slight delay.
So, if you write something like someone maybe leaves a comment on a on a post or something, then the user might not directly see
that comment if it's being from the replicas. Um, so that sometimes give a bit of a struggle and you need to uh, keep an eye
on the replication delay. Maybe the application needs to be able to handle it. You need to monitor it. It's it's a bit of a a hassle.
Um, with the setup, every machine has a complete full copy of all the data. This works fine if it's a few hundred gigabytes, but if you get to the
petabyte range, this doesn't work anymore. So, one of the things people do um, when they're dealing with larger amounts of data is to go for sharding.
That's what you see on the right uh, of this page. So, you have one application and then you're sharding. Maybe it's on like last
name of the customer or some other part of the information you have. And you're splitting up your data. Each part goes into a different
database. Um, this works quite well in basis. However, the application needs to know where what piece of data uh, lives. And for many things like getting back
like a single record related to a single user, this might be easy. But when it comes to analytics, this becomes really hard to work with.
And also the other issue is that maybe one of your customers is really active. And then there's one database that's getting red hot and the other ones are
not doing anything. Um to so to keep all the shards in balance, that can be uh quite uh challenging. So, this is the base problem that we are
trying to solve with TiDB. Um we are already doing this for about 10 years. Um and I think we're quite successful in doing this. So, with TiDB, we get like
one database with reads and writes all going to the same database connection, strongly consistent, fully acid compliant, um and the with ability to get scale
into like many petabyte sizes. Um So, that's what we're trying to accomplish with this uh solution. So, looking at TiDB, we start with uh the SQL layer.
Um so, the SQL layer, of course, gets the SQL queries, knows how [snorts] to execute the SQL queries, and get the results back to the
uh client. We do full SQL support. It's compatible with the same syntax as MySQL is using. Um but the important thing to understand here is that these machines do not store
the data. They only have the uh ability to process SQL queries. And one of them is a primary, so you can write and read to any of them.
With many setups, all the writes have to go to a single machine. Not the case here. You can write to any of them. So, to give an example like how the SQL
looks like that uh we're working with. Um so, as an example, the application that is on the slide here is Mem 9. Mem 9 is a project that we do
including like full text and vector. And then we can just query that in in the normal syntax that you might have seen for like MySQL and other databases.
So we contact the memories table, we filter on two columns, we sort on another column, we're limiting it. It just works as you would expect this to do.
So where is the data actually stored? The data is stored on TiKV. KV stands for key value. So that's part of the whole solution so
you don't have to work with the key value pairs yourself. It just only used behind the scenes. And the the key value store is actually
what makes it a distributed database. Um and this scales the reads and writes. Um another part that we have in the database is the placement driver. This
is a very tiny cluster of machines. And what it does basically is to be the brains of the cluster. So we have a large number of TiKV nodes
and we have a large set of data. And we want to make sure that like every piece of data has like three copies spread out throughout the whole cluster
and that the whole load on the cluster is roughly the same for reads, for writes, but also the data capacity. Um because scaling the cluster is just
done by adding more machines. And the placement driver is basically the one who decides what data goes where. Um so how does storage stays available?
So we split data into data ranges. So one machine holds many data ranges. So these are all parts of of a a table. Uh so one table might be spread out over
many machines. And always there are three copies uh of every piece of data to make sure that if one availability zone goes down the whole cluster still is able to uh
continue process reads, process writes, etc. While this is a really key-value store, we also have the ability to use a co-processor where we send
um basically parts of queries directly to the storage layer. And on the storage layer, we can do some more intelligent filtering, sorting, ordering to like
pre-process the data so we don't have to read everything back to the the SQL layer and process it there. We can already start processing it
um on the uh storage layer. So for example, if you do like a a sum of a whole table, it's not going to send
you back all the all the data and then only then uh on the SQL layer processing it. It it's going to do a sum on each every
storage node. And then um the TiDB layer just combines the result. Um so the the placement driver, the brain, also does some some other parts
that are important for the cluster, including timestamps and keeping some metadata and configuration. Um, and that's also like um, uh, a cluster on itself, uh, based on etcd.
Um, but all this is managed as one big cluster, so it's not that you have to manage all the parts uh, um, itself. Um, one very nice thing,
um, when working with like large volumes of data, is also that we do fully online DDL. So if you schema changes, for example, adding a column, removing a column,
changing a column, or indexes, like maybe adding an index, this is done fully online. So while the index is being added, you can still read and write to the table
uh, without any obstructions. And that's something that many other databases don't do natively or don't do at all. >> Does it ever block any transactions
while you do these DDLs? >> No. All the transactions can just go on and there's no no real impact. So this means that you can actually roll out like a
new version of your application that might have maybe some new tables, some some changes to tables, without having to like wait for like a maintenance
window. And like nowadays maintenance windows are not really there at all. And also like if you make changes on like very large tables, like multiple
hundreds of terabytes, you don't want to wait for the whole change to complete before you actually continue with like the rest of your application.
Um, for those who are who are interested, like the transactions are all MVCC based with a two-phase commit. Um on the Percolator model, um
we have some more information on like the details on on how this works online. >> Yeah, I'll take over from here then. And as Daniel said that we're using Raft
for making sure that we have three copies of the data. When we completed the previous parts, we also realized that this Raft is actually
a change stream as well. And we had some customers that did a bit more analytic queries and so on or started to do table scans,
which is quite costly when it comes to row-based operations cuz you need to read the whole row. So, we figured out that we can actually do columnar search
as well. So, using this Raft stream, we can populate and keep a copy of the data in a columnar format, which means that each column on is
stored by its own, which leads to much higher compression as well as less IO because that's the only thing you need to read. So, we can actually scan things between
20 to 40 times faster. Uh and that also means that we can do big aggregations for a billion row table, for example, in seconds instead
of waiting quite some time. So, all this actually also provides real-time analytics, great for like dashboarding and so on as well. And it's fully in sync and even within
the same transactions. So, compare this to uh streaming the data to ClickHouse or some other analytic tool, for example, first you would have uh
latency for the data copying, as well as you would need another system, so you need to know which system to query. And we have all this fully consistent
even within a single L transaction. And from the SQL, that's basically you can add a a clause that actually does a full table scan as well and filter out
what you want. Here you actually grouping by things that counts 50 times. That's something would take quite some time in a row-based operation, but with
a columnar store, we can make that much much faster. And using the same rough stream, we can also provide an event stream out from
the database into Kafka, for example, or replicate to yet another cluster somewhere else. Uh you can use it for populating your data lake, for example, Snowflake or
even our own new cloud lake. Which means that you can even have event system that triggers on the database changes instead of pulling that through
your own event stream, etc. It can be based on actual bookings, for example, if you have a reservation system, and so on. And that also brings us everyone needs
to pitch to our AI, right? And when you do your own AI stack, this is usually how it looks. You already have your relational
database. You might also throw in document store for the scaling because you have a lot of documents or a lot of data pieces you want to store, and then
the relational database doesn't scale for that really. Uh you might add a graph database for a relational reasoning. Uh did I say relational reasoning? So,
if a relation database can't handle that, well, it actually can. So, you can actually model quite a few of the use cases from graph databases onto
relational databases, and especially in the AI cases. And the reason I'm talking about this is of course the vector database so for semantic search so
if you're searching for cilantro you might want to have coriander as well, right? But that was never found if you would do a text search for example.
And having this as your foundation for AI that means that first of all you have four different systems but you also have data spread around this and most likely need
to be in sync somehow. And that means that you have data pipelines between these four systems so you might actually have at least seven
systems. And how do you handle then the issues when they're out of sync or just one is updated but not the other then that's up
to your application to handle or the AI agent. As well as the AI agent or application needs to know in which order to query
them how to handle that I already filtered out all the results I already got from the first query so I need to redo that.
It's really me means that it's hard to actually put into production. It works perfectly fine in the lab to do this but when you put
it into production and especially at scale that's when things start start to fall apart a bit. So this completely is brittle ETL. It's operation burden high
TCO but also the developer decision paralysis. So how do you actually query this? So that basically led us to first implement vector indexing so we have
vector store and vector indexing as well. That also goes through the same raft stream which means that it's also fully in sync fully consistent. You don't need to
worry about updating it or keeping it up to date and doing batch jobs or anything like that. So adding that to the same query is also
super easy. Order by vector distance. Then you have your embedding column and then the specific vector for your query. So, if you're not aware, that's basically
how a vector search works and semantic search works that you're creating vectors or from your data during with an embedding model. Uh then you get like
maybe vector of 1,500 dimensions. And then you store this in the vector database or in this database with a vector index. And then when you have a query,
you you go through the same embedding model with a query and you get yet another vector. And then you're searching for things in the database that are close to
your actual query distance-wise for the vectors. Which means that you might actually find answers that relates to your query. But that's not all that's needed because
it's fine to have the similar search, but sometimes you also want exact search in the same way. Uh that's why we added full text search
as well. So, you can do like multi-keyword key value search similar to elastic search use cases. And now you can all of a sudden do
hybrid search in the same query. So, you don't need to go to one system for one set of data, another system for another set of data, merge them, and maybe even
find out that okay, I got too little data from both. I didn't have a a good match. So, you need to redo that with
uh a bigger search. And that's what you can add to the same SQL query as well. And FTS match word, so that's the full
text search, really. And then the last piece of our architecture the in the latest version in the cloud our TiDB X our fully managed service is to actually make use
of an object store like Amazon S3 or a blob store something like that. And by using this as the actual source of truth so as soon as we have a
LSM file written we put that into the object store and we can also read that back and cache it back from other storage nodes.
So we have get extremely high durability from that and we also get more or less unlimited bandwidth for scaling. That means that previously generation we
seeded new machines when we're scaling out from the existing storage nodes and that took a little little bit of performance from the existing storage
nodes and we throttled that so we could balance it quite well. But with the object store we can actually read directly from the object
store instead new storage node so it's much faster for scaling out without affecting production at all. And another feature we gain by this is
also this allows a branching of the data so we can actually create a full copy of the whole data the whole database whole cluster and give a way to for
testing or your new agentic AI or something else for experimenting on the same data the full data set without affecting production data at all
so your production can just continue you're creating a new branch and you run your agents versus that or testing and so on and then you can see okay this was
actually uh it's validated my uh experiment so I can put that into production and start using that directly on the production load. So that actually completes the whole
picture. We have an stateless SQL layer that scales really really fast. We can scale it to zero if there's no queries and so on.
We have a row store that handles all the normal transaction load. We have a placement driver that balance the whole storage and also it keeps
our transactions going with their timestamps and so on. The optimizer in the SQL layer is smart enough to know which of the storage types it should read the data from.
So you don't need to know that okay, this is actually a type of analytics query. I need to send this to ClickHouse and this is my normal production load
that goes directly to the relational database and now I'm doing a semantic search and now I need to first fetch the closest vectors in the vector database
and then I need to go also to the full text search and see if I can match the query with the query words that were
specified. You can do this in a single SQL query, right? So you don't need to be the database optimizer. You don't need to be the database
planner. You don't need to be the database executor because if you split all this, then you just have optimizer for each and every part. You don't actually have
it combined. So yet again, you're actually breaking SQL or the query language to small islands instead. Another thing with the object store is also we more or less get backups for
free. The only thing you need to do for the backups is to do a full snapshot of the metadata. Since we're using an LSM tree, all the
files are immutable, so it's very fast to do a full backup as well as a full restore from this. And as you could see, none of this was
actually built from the beginning with AI in mind. Especially not the AI agents that most of us are using daily now. But the properties that makes a good

distributed database, elastic scale, strong consistency, always fresh data, one clean interface like SQL, that's exactly what an agent needs from its data backbone. So, that's the story how we built TiDB
one layer at a time to become the backbone of an AI solution. So, TiDB it speaks SQL, it scales, it's consistent, handles analytics, real-time
analytics as well, has hybrid search, and it's cloud-native as well. And maybe like important to say like it might look very complicated on the
